newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia unveils plans for monopoly reform.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia unveils plans for monopoly reform.

text.p: First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov, drafted into the cabinet last month to help kick-start stalled reforms, on Monday unveiled plans to boost the efficiency of Russia's cumbersome natural monopolies.
Natural monopolies are industries which currently have no competitors, such as gas and electricity, telecommunications and railways.

Nemtsov, who is in charge of restructuring the monopolies, said the government aimed to cut utility prices by introducing competition and increasing state supervision of gas giant Gazprom and national electricity company Unified Energy System.
"This is a truly significant decision showing the basic thrust of government action for restructuring the biggest natural monopolies," he told a news conference.

Restructuring the monopolies is regarded by international lenders like the International Monetary Fund (IMF) as crucial to the success of Russia's market reforms and President Boris Yeltsin on Monday threw his weight behind the plans.

In a decree Yeltsin asked the cabinet to prepare a programme for restructuring, privatising and strengthening state control of natural monopolies and called for the programme to be coordinated among the different government departments.

Nemtsov said Gazprom, the world's biggest gas company and a major supplier to Western European markets, would remain a single entity. Its management has been lobbying hard to prevent any possible breakup of the company.

But Gazprom will have to compete with other companies to exploit new gas reserves in Russia and other gas producers in Russia will be allowed to compete with Gazprom. "We mean equal access to pipelines and equal tariffs for transporting gas."
He said the decree was aimed at strengthening the company's position on international markets. "The richer Gazprom, the richer Russia," Nemtsov said.
The state will also keep control of the national electricity system, retaining its 51 percent stake in UES.
A system of generating companies will be set up and these will sell power at competing prices to a wholesale market which will make it possible to cut electricity charges, Nemtsov said.
Energy from all types of power station, from hydro-electric to nuclear, would be sold on the wholesale market, he added.

He said charges for transporting electricity will be regulated by the Federal Energy Commission, an institution set up by government reformers to bring more competition into the energy sector. There will be a single distribution system.
All electricity producers would have the right to distribute their power on the new network, Nemtsov said.
Government plans include attracting new investment to develop the power system and build new power lines to transmit power from the East to Europe, he said.
"It is necessary to attract investment into UES of $8 billion in the immediate future. That's what we need to do to raise the system to a normal level," he said.
Nemtsov said the government would also retain its controlling stake in Russia's telecom holding company Svyazinvest while opening it up to fresh investment.

Earlier on Monday the presidential press service said Yeltsin had signed a decree authorising the sale of 49 percent of Svyazinvest -- 25 percent and one share at an auction open to foreign and domestic bidders and 24 percent in an investment tender open only to Russian participants.
"(But) government control of Svyazinvest will always be assured," Nemtsov told the news conference.
Nemtsov ruled out privatisation or a breakup of Russia's rail network and said the government would continue to subidise passenger services in the vast country.

However on Monday Yeltsin pledged reform in the thorny area of communal housing, calling in a decree for a shift from the current system of blanket rent subsidies to a more selective targeting of aid for the most needy sections of the population.
